description: Mode design, combat and UI on an external-IP Fortnite game mode at Big Moxi Games.

blocks.html:
Page draft for the portfolio. Lines marked ASSET are things for you to find; brackets are facts to confirm.

Fortnite Game Mode (UEFN) · Big Moxi Games · Published

Turned a UEFN limit into the competitive hook of a published Fortnite mode, designed and pitched with an external IP partner.

rows: Mode design · Combat balance · UI · Usability

blocks.html:
ASSET – Hero video (most important): 60 seconds of a match: a capture fight, the team earning the mech, the activation cutscene, the strike reshaping the map. If you can't capture it, check for an official trailer or the island's preview video.

ASSET – Island code, shown as a button: "Play it in Fortnite". It's your most accessible published work; anyone can try it.

• What I did: designed and pitched the mode with the IP partner, managed combat design and balance, designed the UI from scratch, ran usability tests, and supported production.
  • Hardest problem: UEFN didn't allow players to pilot a mech, which the brief depended on.
  • What it shows: turning a technical limit into a design strength, and keeping an external partner aligned through documentation.

rows: Mode concept and pitch documents · combat balance · UI and HUD design · usability tests
Combat pacing and map features (with level design) · cutscene documentation and storyboard (with concept art)
Production for the team: documentation, presentations, progress reports · animation, art and engineering on the cutscene

blocks.html: Design a competitive Fortnite mode featuring Gundam mechs: a big, cinematic power fantasy that still keeps the match fair and readable for every player.

At the time, UEFN only let players control their own Fortnite character. Piloting a custom vehicle such as a mech wasn't possible, and the brief seemed to depend on it.

There were three obvious responses, and two were dead ends:

rows: Wait for UEFN to support it
No date, and the partner had a schedule
Would feel stiff and break the power fantasy
**Chosen:** the limit becomes the match's goal

blocks.html: [Confirm these were the options the team actually discussed; keep only the true ones.\]

1. The mech is a reward, not a vehicle. Players fight to earn its power, and that fight is the match.
  2. Big moments change the map. A mech strike should matter for the rest of the match, not just look good.
  3. Clear in the chaos. Players always know the objective, who's winning and where the mech will strike.

[Confirm these match the pillars you used; the Wix page lists none.\]

Instead of working around the limit, I made it the centre of the mode. Teams fight to capture points across the map. The leading team earns the mech, a short cinematic sells its scale, and the team chooses which preset zone it strikes, reshaping that part of the map for the rest of the match.

[embedded content: match loop · 5 steps, repeating\]

Why it works

  • The limit drives the match. Teams must keep contesting objectives to earn the mech, so the constraint creates the action instead of slowing it.
  • Decisions that change the map. The winning team chooses where the mech strikes, changing routes and fights from then on.
  • The power fantasy survives. The activation sequence rewards the capture and shows the mech at full scale, with no piloting needed.

ASSET – Map overview: a top-down map marking capture points, the mech spawn area and the strike zones (your documentation image on Wix already shows this).

ASSET – Before/after of one strike zone: two screenshots of the same spot before and after the mech hits it. This is the most convincing image for "decisions that change the map".

I wrote and pitched the mode's design documents to the external IP partner, keeping the brand's needs and the design pillars aligned through approval rounds. With a partner, documentation is how a design survives: every change had to be clear enough to approve without a meeting.

ASSET – Pitch page: one slide or page from the pitch deck, with partner-confidential details blurred.

I managed combat design and balanced the mode, and worked with level design on pacing, engagement routes and implementing gameplay features in the map.

[Add one concrete balance decision, for example how long the mech stays active, how strike zones were sized, or how you stopped the leading team from snowballing. One example turns this from a duty into a decision.\]

I wrote the cutscene's documentation and storyboard with concept artists, and coordinated animation, art and engineering to connect it to live gameplay without breaking the match's flow.

ASSET – Storyboard frames next to the matching in-game frames.

I designed the UI and HUD from scratch with engineering, aiming to keep players oriented and objectives clear during heavy combat: who holds which point, how close each team is to the mech, and where it will strike.

ASSET – HUD screenshot, annotated with 3–4 callouts explaining what each element tells the player.
I ran usability tests to make the mode clearer to players, and kept the team aligned with documentation, presentations and progress reports.

This page has no iteration story yet, and it's the section that matters most at mid-to-senior level. Think back to the usability tests:

  • Problem: \[what players misunderstood or did wrong, for example not knowing which team was close to earning the mech\]
  • Cause: \[why: missing feedback, unclear UI, timing\]
  • Fix: \[what you changed in the UI, the map or the rules\]
  • Result: \[what players did in the next test\]

• Earned mech over fake piloting. Players never steer the mech, which some fans might expect, but the mode gained a clear goal and kept its power fantasy.
  • Preset strike zones over free targeting. \[Confirm the reason, for example keeping map changes balanced and testable.\]

• Published as a Fortnite island with the IP partner.
  • [Plays, players or retention figures, if the partner or Fortnite's creator stats let you share any. Even "X plays in the first week" is valuable.\]

ASSET – Player reactions: 2–3 short comments from players, streamers or the partner, with the source.

What worked: turning the engine limit into the match's goal.

What I'd do differently: \[pick what's true, for example: run usability tests earlier, or prototype the strike zones before writing the cutscene\].

What I learned: an engine limit can become the best idea in the design if you ask what it makes players do; with an external partner, clear documentation is the design.
